source.title: Rethinking Generalization of Neural Models: A Named Entity Recognition Case Study
source.authors: Jin-Lan Fu; Peng-Fei Liu; Qi Zhang; Xuanjing Huang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some tables and figures are flattened or garbled.
record.tranche_reason: Reports original experiments on NER generalization, including fine-grained test performance and annotation corrections, in a task setting not covered by the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates natural-label NER generalization but does not test random-label fitting, width sweeps, the specified optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Cross-domain results are out-of-distribution and excluded from rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports original NER results, but none tests V1–V8. Natural-label NER performance alone does not test memorization capacity alongside generalization; gradient consistency is not magnitude-aware sharpness. Citing Zhang et al. does not make this a test of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors identify NER bottlenecks involving entity coverage, annotation errors, domain and contextual coverage, and category relationships. They report higher measured F1 after jointly correcting training and test annotations, find that more training data does not guarantee better performance, and argue that some category-confusion cases need additional contextual or linguistic knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: NER sequence-labeling analyses and annotation correction; no comparison of random-label memorization and natural-label generalization.
record.method_sensitivity: Test performance varies with entity coverage and pretrained embeddings; the paper also reports context coverage and domain choice as factors, but those cross-domain results are excluded here.

fits_no_version.finding: NER performance varies across entity-coverage groups; the authors report benefits from pretrained representations, especially for unseen entities. Several extracted cells have incorrect subjects or coverage conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NER generalization depends on entity-label coverage and pretrained representations.

fits_no_version.finding: After correcting annotations in 65 test sentences and 14 training sentences, all four reimplemented NER systems obtain higher F1 on revised CoNLL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint correction of training and evaluation annotations can increase measured NER F1.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that gradient-angle category consistency correlates with category error ratios and that low-consistency categories are often confused.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient consistency between NER categories tracks category-confusion patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-domain NER performance tracks entity and contextual coverage; adding source-domain data in different orders produces different performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relevance of source-domain data influences NER transfer performance and the benefit of adding training data.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are stated. Some findings are shown only in figures whose numerical values are unavailable in the supplied text. The paper studies NER-specific generalization and does not test random-label memorization or the other listed interventions.
record.rows_left_out: Cross-dataset generalization results in Exp-III and data augmentation results in Exp-IV use different domains and are out-of-distribution for this claim. Additional Table 4 breakdown values and Table 7 hard-case error rates are omitted to keep the extraction selective; Table 4 contains multiple model-by-coverage entries, while Table 7 is flattened and its model-to-value assignments are not reliably recoverable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label training fit and held-out performance compared with natural labels under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on data size, configuration, or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing examples selected by label-memorization influence versus equal-size random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T3 classification is incorrect because none of the specified versions is tested. All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, even where the underlying NER finding is clear. Out-of-distribution results are outside these versions because they measure different relationships, not because such settings are categorically ineligible.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fit random labels or compare random-label and natural-label test performance for the same architectures and recipes.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected image classifiers.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with the specified generalization measures.
Does not remove memorized training examples.

rows.subject: CNN, Rand
rows.operation_detail: Breaks down CoNLL test F1 by entity coverage ratio.
rows.note: Row reports natural-label test performance; it does not test random-label fitting.
rows.check: Table 4 places 76.42 in the Overall column, not the ρ=1 column. The flattened table also makes the stated CNN/Rand subject assignment uncertain. This F1 score cannot establish any listed version.

rows.subject: CNN, Rand
rows.operation_detail: Breaks down CoNLL test F1 by entity coverage ratio.
rows.note: The authors state unseen entities achieve lower performance in general.
rows.check: 69.74 appears under ρ=0 with C≠0, not C=0. The CNN/Rand subject assignment also needs checking against the flattened model labels. Lower subgroup F1 is not a partial instance of any listed version.

rows.note: Unseen-entity score is lower than the same-label-seen score.
rows.check: 77.83 is the fourth model entry under ρ=0 with C≠0, corresponding to BERT, rather than FLAIR/GloVe with C=0. No listed version is measured.

rows.subject: FLAIR, GloVe
rows.note: The paper states that FLAIR and ELMo improve unseen-entity performance.
rows.check: Overall FLAIR/GloVe F1 of 93.03 is supported by Tables 4 and 5, but does not establish any listed version.

rows.subject: FLAIR, GloVe
rows.operation_detail: Measures CoNLL test F1 for entities seen in training with a different or diverse label.
rows.note: The authors describe this coverage group as the most challenging.
rows.check: 86.66 is the fourth model entry in the ρ∈(0,0.5] column, corresponding to BERT. It is not FLAIR/GloVe performance for C≠0. Diverse-label entities and entities never seen with the test label are distinct groups.

rows.subject: FLAIR, GloVe
rows.operation_detail: Retrains the NER model after correcting annotations in the training and test data.
rows.note: The table gives original CoNLL and revised ReCoNLL scores; the paper says all listed models improved after corrections.
rows.check: The 93.03→93.78 comparison is correct, but both training and test annotations changed; it is not an isolated training-data intervention. It measures none of V1–V8.

rows.subject: GloVe
rows.operation_detail: Retrains the NER model after correcting annotations in the training and test data.
rows.note: The table gives original CoNLL and revised ReCoNLL scores.
rows.check: The 89.10→89.85 comparison is correct. GloVe identifies the embedding configuration of an NER system, not a standalone model. Both training and test annotations changed, and no listed version is measured.

rows.subject: ELMo
rows.operation_detail: Retrains the NER model after correcting annotations in the training and test data.
rows.note: The table gives original CoNLL and revised ReCoNLL scores.
rows.check: The 91.79→92.65 comparison is correct, but both training and test annotations changed. This does not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: BERT
rows.operation_detail: Retrains the NER model after correcting annotations in the training and test data.
rows.note: Table lists BERT at 92.22 on CoNLL and 92.65 on ReCoNLL.
rows.check: Table 5's own BERT implementation improves from 91.34 to 92.16. The baseline 92.22 is a cited ELMo result, while 92.65 is the revised ELMo result. The recorded comparison mixes subjects and attribution.

rows.subject: CcnnWglovecnnMlp
rows.operation_detail: Compares category-level consistency with category error rates.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between consistency values and error values
rows.note: The text says consistency values correlate closely with error ratios but gives no numeric coefficient in the supplied text.
rows.check: Gradient-angle consistency versus category error ratios does not measure V7's magnitude-scaled weight perturbations or training–test gaps. Figure 3's numeric coefficient and model-specific attribution cannot be reliably read from the supplied text.

rows.subject: NER models trained on CoNLL; individual model not stated
rows.operation_detail: Relates category consistency values to cross-category prediction errors.
rows.measure: Association between category consistency and errors between categories
rows.value: The model tends to have difficulty distinguishing low-consistency categories and can mis-predict them as each other.
rows.note: Qualitative result; the paper says consistency values correlate closely with error ratios.
rows.check: The qualitative association is stated in Exp-VI, but category confusion and gradient consistency do not measure any listed version.
